title: Leader Election Patterns
description: Compare bully algorithm, ring election, lease-based election with fencing tokens, and how Chubby prevents split-brain at Google.

segments.text: Every distributed system that uses a leader eventually faces the same question: what happens when the leader dies? Leader election is the process of choosing a new leader, and getting it wrong means either no leader, which stalls the system, or two leaders, which corrupts your data. Let's look at the patterns that solve this.

The bully algorithm is the simplest approach. Every node has an ID. When a node detects the leader is down, it sends election messages to all nodes with higher IDs. If no higher-ID node responds, it declares itself leader. If any responds, that higher node takes over. The highest-ID node always wins, hence 'bully.' It's O of n squared messages but dead simple.

Ring election arranges nodes in a logical ring. When a node detects the leader is down, it sends an election message around the ring. Each node appends its ID and forwards. When the message returns to the initiator, the node with the highest ID in the message is elected. It uses O of n messages but takes O of n time to complete.

Both algorithms have a fundamental problem: they assume reliable failure detection. But in a distributed system, you can't distinguish between a dead node and a slow network. Node A thinks the leader is dead and starts an election. But the leader is fine, just experiencing network delays. Now you have two nodes thinking they're the leader. Split-brain.
segments.thought_prompt: If you can't reliably detect whether a node is dead or just slow, how can you ever safely elect a new leader?

segments.text: Lease-based election solves this elegantly. The leader holds a lease: a time-bounded lock. 'I am the leader for the next 10 seconds.' The leader must renew before the lease expires. If it fails to renew, other nodes know the lease expired and can safely elect a new leader. The old leader also knows its lease expired and stops acting as leader.

But leases alone aren't enough. Imagine: the old leader's process pauses for a garbage collection during its lease. It resumes after the lease expired, not knowing time passed. It still thinks it's the leader and writes data. Fencing tokens fix this. Each lease comes with a monotonically increasing token. The storage layer rejects writes with old tokens.

Here's how fencing works concretely. Leader A gets lease with token 33. Leader A pauses. Lease expires. Leader B gets lease with token 34. Leader A resumes and tries to write with token 33. The storage sees token 33 is less than current token 34 and rejects the write. Data integrity preserved. This is why Martin Kleppmann considers fencing tokens essential.
segments.thought_prompt: What happens if the storage layer doesn't support fencing token checks? Can you still prevent split-brain?

segments.text: Google's Chubby lock service implements lease-based leader election at massive scale. Applications acquire a Chubby lock with a sequencer, Google's version of a fencing token. Chubby itself runs Paxos internally with five replicas across data centers. BigTable, MapReduce, and GFS all use Chubby for leader election. It's the coordination backbone of Google's infrastructure.

In practice today, most teams don't implement leader election from scratch. They use etcd's election API, ZooKeeper's leader election recipe, or Consul's session-based locking. The implementation is done for you. But understanding the underlying patterns, leases, fencing tokens, quorum-based election, is essential for debugging when things go wrong at three AM.

Leader election is deceptively hard because the failure modes are subtle. Network partitions, GC pauses, clock skew: each can create split-brain if you're not careful. Leases bound the window of uncertainty. Fencing tokens prevent stale leaders from doing damage. Together, they make leader election safe in the real world, not just in theory.
